new_statements.quote: Betonung der Wörter. In dem einzeln gesprochenen Worte herrscht beim Substantivum und Adjectivum das Bestreben vor, die letzte Silbe zu betonen, im Zusammenhang der Rede aber scheint der Accent keiner bestimmten Silbe anzugehören. Durch das Betonen der letzten Silbe wird ein schnelles Hinweggleiten der Stimme über die Anfangssilben bedingt, und daher sind hier lange Vocale sowie Doppelconsonanten, welche beide ein Verweilen der Stimme bedingen, selten. Diese Hastigkeit der Sprache erschwert das Erfassen der Vocale der ersten Silben ungemein [...]
new_statements.translation: Word stress. In the word spoken in isolation, nouns and adjectives show a prevailing tendency to stress the last syllable; in connected speech, however, the accent seems to belong to no particular syllable. Stressing the last syllable causes the voice to glide quickly over the initial syllables, and therefore long vowels and double consonants, both of which require the voice to linger, are rare there. This hastiness of the language makes it extremely hard to catch the vowels of the first syllables [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation forms, nouns and adjectives tend to carry prominence on the final syllable, with reduced/hurried pretonic syllables; in connected speech no fixed stress position is discernible. (Pre-tonal 1886 description based on Krause's notes from displaced speakers; modern descriptions — Tourneux 1978, 1991 — analyse Musgu/Munjuk as a tone language with H, L, rising and falling tonemes and make no statement about stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Statement restricted to nouns and adjectives in isolation; in connected speech 'the accent seems to belong to no particular syllable'; in the copular/verbalised paradigm Müller notes (p. ~378) that 'der Ton' may also rest on the subject verbal pronoun. Krause marks accent ad hoc with an acute in some transcriptions (e.g. tsémana, proper names).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation (isolation) forms of nouns/adjectives only; explicitly not phrase-level. Source predates tonal analysis; what Krause heard as final 'Betonung' may reflect tone/final prominence in a language now described as tonal (Tourneux 1978 ch. 3: 'Chaque syllabe, en mulwi, est affectée d'un ton'; Tourneux 1991: 'Le munjuk est une langue à tons').
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Müller 1886) rests on G. A. Krause's notes taken in Tripoli from freed Musgu ('Musuk') slaves, chiefly Ali Mut of Ngilemong village near Kadé on the Logone (Cameroon-side Musgu proper, musg1254). The modern descriptions examined cover other varieties of the same language: Tourneux 1978 = Mulwi/Vulum of Mogroum (Chad; Glottolog dialect 'Vulum'), Tourneux 1991 = Munjuk 'des rizières', Pouss dialect (Cameroon; 'Mpus'). All fall under musg1254.

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict. Müller/Krause 1886 (already in existing_statements) reports a tendency to stress the final syllable of isolated nouns and adjectives with no fixed accent in connected speech, for the Cameroon Musuk; Tourneux 1978 describes the Chad Mulwi/Vulum of Mogroum purely in terms of four tonemes on two registers and says nothing about stress or accent. The two sources talk past each other (an 1880s 'Betonung' report from a non-linguist's notes versus a 1978 tonological analysis of a different dialect), so the catalog's existing final-stress reading rests on Müller 1886 alone and is not supported or refuted by the modern description.

sources.note: Section 'Betonung der Wörter' (p. 359): in words spoken in isolation, nouns and adjectives tend to stress the last syllable; in connected speech the accent seems to belong to no particular syllable; final stress makes the voice hurry over initial syllables, so long vowels and geminates are rare there. Elsewhere (verbal 'to be' paradigm) notes 'der Ton' can also rest on the subject pronoun; acute marks accent in transcriptions.
